newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian currency woes drag on...and on.
newsitem.headline: Asian currency woes drag on...and on.

text.p: Asian currencies came under renewed pressure again on Thursday with the Thai baht's fall to a record low leading the regional currencies a little further on the downward spiral.
The baht slumped to new lows after a swathe of bad news from the financial sector where cash flow problems have savaged balance sheets.
Of 18 finance and securities firms reporting half year figures, only seven made a profit and the sector's losses as a whole totalled a depressing 3.5 billion baht (US$108 million).
However, what may have started as a speculative attack on Southeast Asian these currencies has turned into a rush to hedge, analysts said.

"It's a brave man who speculates in these markets now," said Tim Lucas, treasury manager at Bank of Bermuda in Hong Kong. "What's happening now is genuine portfolio hedging and genuine concern as opposed to having a speculative play."

The onshore baht rate crunched down to 32.50, making its loss on the U.S. dollar so far this year a bumper 21.5 percent. The Singapore dollar dipped to a 33-month low of 1.4785 and the Malaysian ringgit fell to a 38-month low of 2.6530 to the U.S.
dollar.
The Sing dollar's slip this morning led Thursday's action, but it is the Thai baht which is in the driving seat from a regional point of view.

"This impact on regional currencies is certainly being led by Thailand," said Christa Marti, senior economist at UBS in Singapore. "And there's going to be a lot of bad news to come in terms of economic fundamentals. The slowdown has only just started."
The sharp lack of confidence and the absence of a clear-cut government package to stop the economic rot will drive the baht lower, Marti said.

"The only thing at this stage that can help the baht is if an external aid package is announced. Any internal measures, unless they are revolutionary, are not going to help the market. They have to buy credibility externally, from the IMF for example," she added.
Even North Asian currencies, immune to the turmoil until now, caught a cold with the Hong Kong dollar forward rates shooting up as traders sold it forward.
While some of this reflected speculative selling, there was also considerable fund hedging, dealers said.
"There are more fund managers per square inch in Hong Kong than anywhere else in the world. People are being prudent and covering themselves for a portion of their portfolio," said one trader.
Analysts said a lot of the action in other Asian currencies reflected continued hedging by nervous investors who thus far had only had partially hedged positions.
For example, the Indonesia rupiah had steadily declined for years under a government managed depreciation so investors knew exactly where they were.
The high yield more than compensated for the decline in the currency so a prudent fund manager would only have hedged a portion of his portfolio, certainly not all of it.
But, analysts said some portfolios are now approaching a 100 percent hedge in some parts of the region as their trustees and shareholders remain highly nervous.

Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad launched a bitter attack on "rogue speculators' at the opening of the nine-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday.
"We see a well-planned effort to undermine the economies of all the ASEAN countries by destabilising their currencies," he told the meeting.
But blaming speculators at this stage may be pointing the finger a the wrong people, analysts said.
